newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Interior ministry seeks Russia interest rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Interior ministry seeks Russia interest rate cut.

text.p: The Interior Ministry, linking high yields on government securities to rising Russian crime, has called on the authorities to cut interest rates, but did not say how its plan could work.
An Interior Ministry report published by Nezavisimaya Gazeta on Friday said interest rates on short-term government securities should fall to a "normal profit" rate of 10 percent.
The bills currently yield 30-36 percent, well above December's year-on-year inflation rate of almost 22 percent, but well below rates around 200 percent in May last year.
Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov said the report reflected his ministry's views.
"We are being blamed for interfering in economic issues, but how can we fail to do so where we see criminalisation on the rise in the economy," Kulikov told a news conference.
The interior ministry is responsible for fighting crime in Russia but has no influence on monetary policy.
The newspaper said Russian President Boris Yeltsin, in hospital with pneumonia, had received a copy of the report.
It was not clear how the ministry thought the govenrment could sell securities at 10 percent and the report said only that "compensatory measures should be taken to avoid a fall in demand".
The ministry also said Russian enterprises should lose their right to hold accounts in convertible currencies and be obliged to sell all hard currency revenues to the central bank.
Many Russian exporters have dollar accounts for foreign trade operations, and they must sell half of their foreign currency revenues on the open market.
The document said its proposals "would help de-dollarise the economy and strengthen the rouble".
Dollars received by the state under the new regulations would be placed abroad at high interest rates, creating additional sources of revenue.
The ministry said the number of economic crimes in the banking sector had more than trebled last year and it urged the government to crack down on these.
It was not the interior ministry's first attempt to change Russian economic policy.

Kulikov last February advocated nationalising some commercial banks and reintroducing oil export tariffs to raise money for the army and for his ministry, whose troops were active in breakaway Chechnya.
